newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish government survives Rushdie row.
newsitem.headline: Danish government survives Rushdie row.

text.p: Denmark's minority government emerged bloodied but intact on Thursday from a row over a visit by British author Salman Rushdie that nearly brought it down.

Left-wing parties which would have held the casting votes in a threatened vote of no confidence declared Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen clumsy and inept but not to be pursuing a hidden political agenda as they had feared.

"I now see the case as solely one in which Nyrup and his people have bungled and a blunder is not something on which we would topple the government," Socialist People's Party leader Holger Nielsen told Det Fri Aktuelt daily.
Rushdie was told he could not come to Denmark to receive a literary prize because his safety could not be guaranteed.
The government backed down after an uproar but its political opponents initially suspected Rasmussen's real motive was an effort to appease important trade partner Iran.

Rushdie has lived in hiding and under guard since 1989 when Iranian revolutionary leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini issued a fatwa or death sentence against him for his novel "The Satanic Verses", saying it blasphemed against Islam.
Iran imported 1.2 billion crowns worth of Danish feta-type cheese in 1991-92, but sales have declined because of importers' bad debts which Danish producers are trying to recover.
After attending a session of the secret parliamentary intelligence oversight committee on Wednesday Nielsen said he believed that there had been a real security threat to Rushdie.

Denied a majority without the left, the rightist camp will now drop its plan to oust Nyrup but is likely to win cross-party support for harsh censure of the government at a debate next week, political sources from both sides said.
A Gallup poll taken at the height of the storm showed Rasmussen's Social Democrats plunging to their lowest approval rating since December 1988, when they were in opposition.

Asked how they would vote if an election were held now, only 29.1 percent of respondents chose the Social Democrats, compared to 34.6 in the 1994 general election said the poll, published in the Danish daily Berlingske Tidende.
In a real election that would reduce their parliamentary seats to 53 from their current 62. The poll showed the Socialist People's Party expanding to 18 seats from 13 at present.
The centre-left government, with support from the left would still outvote the right-wing opposition forces by a combined 93 seats to 85 in the 179-seat assembly.

Rasmussen has admitted that his government mishandled the Rushdie affair, in which the writer was told of the entry ban in a press statement while his associates were still in planning talks with Danish authorities for a trip they thought approved.
Rasmussen said that public knowledge of the writer's plan to attend the November 14 award ceremony in Copenhagen -- this year's European Cultural Capital -- would threaten his safety.
Following an outcry at home and abroad he apologised and said that the message to Rushdie had omitted an offer to find an alternative date on which to receive his prize.
